title: Please Listen to How Plasma Waste Converters Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain plasma waste treatment (plasma gasification and pyrolysis). They cover how lightning-like plasma is made, how plasma torches break garbage down into syngas, slag, and heat without combustion, and how syngas can drive gas turbines and steam generators to produce electricity. They discuss cleaning syngas, the heavy metal hazards, slag uses (paving stones, rock wool for insulation and oil spill cleanup), radioactive waste vitrification, the handful of operating plants worldwide, economic and landfill-competition issues, and ideas like co-locating with coal plants and decontaminating livestock or soil. The episode ends with a listener letter correcting their language about Africa and puberty episode feedback.

entities.name: Stuff You Should Know episode on lightning

segments.title: Opening banter and plasma explained
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, then explain lightning-generated superheated air and plasma as the fourth state of matter, including molecular dissociation and pyrolysis.

segments.title: What plasma torches can do with garbage
segments.summary: Plasma torches can break down waste without combustion or oxygen, turning organics into syngas and metals into slag, and can recover more energy from garbage than incineration.

segments.title: Plant design: feedstock, furnace, and plasma torch
segments.summary: Plants are custom built; conveyor belts feed pretreated waste into an airtight furnace with a water-cooled plasma torch, slag drains, gas venting, and a coke bed that keeps the furnace hot. The torch uses an electric arc to heat air to plasma.

segments.title: Generating electricity from syngas
segments.summary: Syngas expands through a gas turbine, then a heat recovery steam generator makes steam for another turbine, and syngas can also fuel an engine, so the plant can power itself and sell electricity.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a short break with banter.

segments.title: Cleaning syngas and hazardous byproducts
segments.summary: Syngas is water scrubbed and filtered, with an afterburner possible. Heavy metals such as cadmium and mercury must be removed, and about 20 tons of residue remain per 1,000 tons of waste.

segments.title: Uses for slag and rock wool
segments.summary: Slag weighs the same as the original waste's inert portion, about 5 percent of volume, and can be used in asphalt, concrete, and paving stones. Compressed air turns molten slag into rock wool for hydroponics, insulation, and oil spill cleanup. Radioactive material can be vitrified into stable glass, and the hosts discuss vaseline glass.

segments.title: Operating plants, costs, and landfill competition
segments.summary: About eight plasma gasification facilities operated worldwide, including in Japan, Canada, England, the US, India, China, and one on a US aircraft carrier. A Port St. Lucie, Florida project was planned; a Utashinai, Japan plant closed when it ran out of feedstock; a large plant cost about half a billion dollars. Costs, tipping fees, and competition with landfills are discussed.

segments.title: Future ideas: landfill mining, coal plant co-location, decontamination
segments.summary: Dr. Cerczio of Georgia Tech envisions plasma torches inserted into landfills and co-located with coal plants to burn waste and reduce fossil fuel use. Hosts also joke about decontaminating diseased livestock, contaminated soil, and medical waste, and about the Centralia coal fire.

segments.title: Listener mail: Africa and puberty episode feedback
segments.summary: A listener from Ghana praises the female puberty episode and asks hosts to be specific when discussing regions, noting Africa is a continent of many countries and cultures. Josh and Chuck acknowledge the feedback and the boy crazy comment.
